Alternatively, if read narrowly as a named-road consent ("via Bedok North Road"), nothing in the fact table ties the driven track to that road or to any other road, which is exactly the G13 situation — undetermined scope [F9][F10]. Because the segment's treatment is the same either way (no amount attaches to it on either reading, and it is not an "unexempted" segment), the record does not need this element to be settled to reach the outcome, and I leave the scope finding undetermined rather than converting an unresolved consent question into a refund [RD-5]. The rider advocate itself concedes this segment [C2, C3, D3]; the driver's concession that it was rider-agreed routing supports no refund on it [RD-5].

Segment 2 [F4]: the chat is complete and fully timestamped, containing two messages only [F11]. No rider message before 17:18:05 agrees to this turn-off; the rider's only message is F10 at 17:02, seven minutes before this segment began and limited to the jam round the start [F10]. claims.assertion: Two off-route segments are recorded on this metered RydeTAXI trip: 17:04–17:11 added 2.44 km and 17:18–17:23 added 2.58 km (total 5.02 km), against an overall excess of +5.4 km over the 16.3 km optimal route.

The 17:04–17:11 segment is covered by the rider's consent: the driver asked at 17:01 whether he could 'go round via Bedok North Road' and the rider replied at 17:02 'Sure, your call.' — a message sent before the segment started, so consent was given in advance.

That consent only reaches the named deviation discussed ('Bedok North Road'); it is at most a specific-route authorisation and cannot be stretched to a second, later deviation the rider never agreed to.

The 17:18–17:23 segment is an unexempted off-route segment: it began 7 minutes after the consented segment ended, the rider sent nothing further, and the driver's own written statement admits 'The second turn-off was my GPS rerouting.'

No 'reasonable cause' exemption applies to the 17:18–17:23 segment: no traffic incidents were recorded near the route during the trip window (only band-4 conditions of 30–39 km/h on PIE and CTE, which cannot exempt a segment on their own, and fair weather).

The driver's claim that the rider agreed to the second turn-off is not consent — it appears only in his post-trip statement (a verbal/asserted agreement, unsupported by any rider message) and no chat message by the rider covers the 17:18–17:23 segment.

Because this is a metered RydeTAXI trip, the unexempted segment's extra kilometres entered the fare: the unexempted 2.58 km × $1.4100/km = $3.6378, i.e. $3.64 refundable, computed from the billed per-km rate of $1.4100.

Only the metre units of the unexempted segment are refundable; the waiting charge of $0.13 for 0.5 min is metre waiting time and is not refundable, and the remaining unallocated mileage difference is not claimed.

The driver already has 2 upheld route disputes in the last 90 days (route: 2), so this second upheld route deviation makes the conduct repeated and warrants sending the driver's account for review alongside the refund.

weaknesses: The chat only shows a general/short reply ('Sure, your call.'), which the driver will argue was a general route authorisation covering his own routing choices for the whole trip; if the judge reads it that widely, the 17:18–17:23 segment could be treated as consented (F10).

There is no record tying the consented 'Bedok North Road' route to the driven track, so the driver may argue the first segment's scope was never limited to that named road; that does not extinguish my claim on the second segment, but it weakens the neat split between segment 1 and segment 2 (F9, F3, F4).

The driver's statement that the second turn-off was 'my GPS rerouting' could invite an argument that a congestion-driven reroute happened, but the only traffic facts are band-4 (30–39 km/h) and no incidents, which cannot exempt a segment under RD-4 (F13, F14, F15).
The exact refund figure depends on the per-km rate derived from this trip's own fare facts ($1.4100/km per F5); if Ryde computes the metered rate differently, the amount may shift slightly (F5, F8).

claims.assertion: This is a RydeTAXI metered trip (F8: base $3.90, distance $30.54 for 21.66 km, time $8.65, platform $1.47), so under RD-2 any deviation refund is limited to unexempted extra_km × this trip's per-km rate of $1.4100 (F5), i.e. only the metered mileage units — not the whole excess fare and not the waiting time.

There are exactly two off-route segments: 17:04–17:11 adding 2.44 km (F3) and 17:18–17:23 adding 2.58 km (F4); RD-1 requires each to be reviewed separately, so only the second can be contested by the rider.

The first segment (F3) is covered by rider consent given before it started: the driver asked at 17:01 'ok if I go round via Bedok North Road?' (F9) and the rider replied at 17:02 'Sure, your call.' (F10), both timestamps earlier than the F3 segment start of 17:04.

The rider's 'Sure, your call.' (F10) is a general route authorisation ('your call' on how to get there, unprompted by any driver-side errand), which under RD-5 covers the route chosen to reach the destination, including the 17:04–17:11 diversion round the building congestion — so that segment yields no refund (no_action as to it).

Even if the consent in F10 were read narrowly as a named-road consent ('via Bedok North Road', F9), it still cannot be defeated by the rider here: the rider is the party relying on the deviation and no record ties the F3 driven segment to any road other than the one the rider agreed to, so at worst that segment is undetermined rather than an unexempted deviation (G13).

The driver's congestion reason for the first diversion is corroborated by the traffic record: the Pan Island Expressway — the expressway named in F9 — was at speed band 4 (30–39 km/h) during 16:49–17:38 (F13), covering the 17:04–17:11 segment.

The second segment (17:18–17:23, +2.58 km, F4) has no rider consent: no chat message authorises it, there are only two messages in a complete, fully timestamped record (F11), and the driver's post-trip statement that 'the second turn-off was my GPS rerouting' (F12) is a statement, not consent — RD-5 requires the rider's own message sent before the segment started, and it does not exist.

No exemption is available for the second segment: there is no traffic incident near the route during the trip window (F15), weather was fair with 0.0 mm rain (F16), and band 4 (30–39 km/h) congestion on PIE (F13) or Central Expressway (F14) is not the band 1–2 severe congestion RD-4(b) contemplates and in any event does not excuse an unmatched segment.

The refund on the single unexempted segment is 2.58 km × $1.4100/km = $3.64 SGD (rounded to the cent), using the extra_km of the F4 segment and this trip's distance fare ÷ distance km of $1.4100 (F5).

The rider's request cannot reach the other $3.92 of billed excess: the fare fact bills $7.56 for 5.36 km of excess (F5), while the exempt first segment (2.44 km, F3) and undetermined-road second segment aside, no further unexempted kilometre is established, and RD-2 expressly does not refund mileage outside the identified unexempted segments.

The billed waiting fee of $0.13 (F6: 0.5 min × $0.26/min) is a metered waiting unit on a RydeTAXI trip and is not refundable under RD-3(c), and the first segment was a rider-requested/agreed routing (F9, F10) on which the stop time is treated the same way.

weaknesses: The GPS record is the decisive evidence against my client: 21.7 km actual vs 16.3 km optimal, +5.4 km / +33% (F1), and 33.8 min vs the 23.4 min estimate (F2) — the overall picture is a materially longer trip than the quote, and the rider will lead with F1 and F2.

The second segment itself is hard to defend: 3.48 km driven where the optimal route covers 0.89 km, +2.58 km, up to 1163 m off route (F4), with no rider consent message (F11) — the driver's 'my GPS rerouting' explanation (F12) is a post-trip statement and, per G11/RD-5, does not constitute consent, so a refund of 2.58 km × $1.41 = $3.64 is likely to be ordered.

My reading of 'Sure, your call.' (F10) as a general route authorisation covering the whole trip is contestable: the rider's own complaint says the second turn-off was not agreed, and a judge may read F9/F10 as scoped to the named road 'Bedok North Road' only (F9) — leaving the F3 segment, with 2.44 km extra (F3), open to the same treatment as F4 under RD-5/G13, which would raise the refund toward $7.11.

The driver's congestion justification has no incident support at all: no traffic incidents were recorded near the route in the trip window (F15), so RD-4(a) is unavailable and the band-4 speeds (F13, F14) are only corroborative and, per RD-4(b)/G3, do not exempt a segment on their own.

The driver's profile is the main flag_account risk: 2 route disputes upheld in 90 days (F18), so with a refund > 0 this case makes the finding 'repeated' under RD-6 and account-review is likely — a point the rider can press even though profile facts cannot decide the deviation itself.

This cuts both ways: if no record ties the 17:04-17:11 segment to 'Bedok North Road' (F9, F3), the consent scope for that segment is undetermined under G13 - but that undetermined segment carries 2.44 km, while my claim rests on the separate 2.58 km segment at 17:18-17:23 (F4), which no consent message of any scope covers.
